tldr: Tool-integrated reasoning failures often stem from misaligned tool-use patterns (calculator vs. algorithmic); a two-stage framework building code competence then aligning pattern preferences with DPO substantially improves both code reliability and accuracy on math benchmarks.
contributions: Identification and formalization of pattern mismatch in TIR, showing misaligned tool-use strategies derail otherwise sound reasoning.
A two-stage learning framework: (1) code competence acquisition via SFT on both calculator and algorithmic patterns, and (2) pattern preference alignment via DPO with teacher signals.
Empirical results on MATH500, AIME24, GSM8K, and R1Math demonstrating substantial gains in Code@1 and Pass@1.
methods: The authors define two tool-use patterns: calculator-pattern (Python as a direct computation/verification tool) and algorithmic-pattern (encoding problems as full programs). In Stage 1 (Code Competence Acquisition), the model is trained via SFT on paired solutions using both patterns, minimizing negative log-likelihood over response tokens. In Stage 2 (Pattern Preference Alignment), a teacher model (Gemini-2.5-flash-lite) labels a preferred and dispreferred solution for each problem, and DPO is applied with a frozen SFT reference policy to align pattern selection with teacher preferences.
results: Code@1 on MATH500 improved from 64.0% to 70.5%; AIME24 Pass@1 rose from 26.7% to 50.0%; GSM8K Code@1 increased from 72.0% to 80.1%; AIME24 Code+Pass@1 improved from 6.6% to 26.7%. R1Math Code@1 reached 72.2% and Pass@1 reached 55.5% after SFT+DPO.
limitations: The approach relies on a teacher model (Gemini-2.5-flash-lite) to generate labels, which may introduce bias or errors. The paper evaluates primarily on math benchmarks (MATH500, AIME24, GSM8K, AMC23) without demonstrating generalization to non-mathematical tool-use scenarios. Base model performance on AIME24 was near zero (0.0% Code@1), suggesting limitations for harder or more diverse problem types.
